input:
Effective inventory management requires that adequate safety stock be held in order to protect the organisation against the uncertainties that are inherent in demand, and in the case of the spare motor that is considered here, the safety stock requirement has been determined to be 1952 units. This stock is held in order to cover the variation in demand that can arise during the replenishment lead time, and it is based on a cycle service level of 95%.

The demand for the spare motor is characterised by a mean demand of 1830 units per week and a standard deviation of 483 units per week, while the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. On the basis of these figures, and taking into account the fact that the stock must cover the variability of demand accumulated over the entire lead time rather than the variability of any single week, the safety stock of 1952 units is the quantity that is required in order to achieve the desired 95% cycle service level.

A number of assumptions underpin this policy. In particular, demand is treated as being normally distributed and independent from one week to the next, an assumption that is of considerable importance because it allows the variations in individual weeks to offset one another to some degree over the course of the lead time. Furthermore, seasonal peaks in demand are excluded from the analysis, which means that no additional provision has been made for periods of unusually high demand, and any peak that happens to arise within a lead time must be accommodated from the safety stock that is available.
target:
Safety stock for the spare motor is 1952 units. The stock covers variation in demand during the replenishment lead time at a 95% cycle service level.

Demand for the spare motor averages 1830 units per week, with a standard deviation of 483 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. The safety stock is sized on the spread of demand over the whole lead time: weekly demand varies around its mean, and the stock has to absorb the accumulated variation across the full lead time, not the variation of a single week. At a 95% cycle service level, demand during the lead time is met from stock in all but a small minority of replenishment cycles, and 1952 units is the holding that the stated demand spread requires for that level.

The policy treats demand as normal and independent between weeks. Independence is the assumption that lets weekly variations partly cancel over the lead time; if demand in successive weeks moved together, the spread of lead-time demand would be wider and the same stock would return a lower service level. Seasonal peaks are excluded. No separate stock is held for peak periods, and a peak that falls inside a lead time draws on the safety stock in the same way as any other demand, so the stated service level describes ordinary variation across the year and not peak cover.

The figure is reviewed when the demand pattern or the lead time changes.
